courseTitle: Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Generative AI Fundamentals for Data Scientists

slots.practicalActivity: In a notebook, reproduce the lesson's neuron-as-regression demo: compute z = x @ w + b and a sigmoid activation by hand with numpy, then build the make_circles ring dataset and compare a plain LogisticRegression against an MLPClassifier with 1 hidden layer. Rerun the MLP with hidden_layer_sizes of 2, 4, and 8 neurons and record how held-out accuracy changes as capacity grows.
slots.deliverable: A notebook cell printing the logistic-regression vs. MLP accuracy gap on the ring data, plus a small table of accuracy at 2, 4, and 8 hidden neurons.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement a tiny 3-input, 4-hidden, 1-output forward pass in raw numpy (random W1/b1, W2/b2, ReLU activation), and confirm that removing the activation collapses two stacked layers into one linear transform (np.allclose check). Then compute binary cross-entropy by hand for predicted probabilities of 0.9, 0.5, and 0.1 against a true label of 1, and compare the loss values.
slots.deliverable: A script producing the hidden-layer output, the np.allclose(True) proof that activations matter, and the 3 cross-entropy values with a one-line explanation of why confident wrong answers cost more.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's 1-8-1 tanh network in numpy on a noisy sine wave, implement the forward/backward/update loop by hand, and verify your backprop gradient against a numerical (finite-difference) gradient check to at least 6 digits of agreement. Then refit the same curve with sklearn's MLPRegressor and, if time allows, a 3-line PyTorch version, comparing final loss across all three implementations.
slots.deliverable: A notebook showing the analytic-vs-numerical gradient match, a loss curve over training epochs, and a 3-row comparison table (numpy / scikit-learn / PyTorch) of final MSE on the same sine data.

lessons.title: When Neural Networks Beat Classical ML

slots.practicalActivity: Train an intentionally oversized 200-200 neuron MLPRegressor on 60 noisy sine points with alpha=0 and alpha=0.1, and record the train/test MSE gap for each. Then run the chapter's fair head-to-head comparison (logistic regression, HistGradientBoostingClassifier, and an MLP) with 5-fold cross-validation across a real dataset (load_breast_cancer or load_digits) and an invented threshold-rule tabular dataset, confirming which model wins on which data shape.
slots.deliverable: A table of train/test MSE at alpha=0 vs. alpha=0.1 for the overfitting demo, plus a 3-model x 2-dataset accuracy table with a 3-sentence written decision checklist for when you would reach for a neural network instead of boosted trees.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's tiny RNN in numpy, scale its recurrent weight matrix to a 0.9 spectral radius, and measure how much a nudge to the first token in a sequence affects the final hidden state at lengths 2, 5, 10, 20, and 40 steps, confirming the vanishing-gradient pattern. Then hand-build the 4-token attention example (query/key/value dot products plus softmax) and verify which earlier word the attention weights point to.
slots.deliverable: A printed table of signal-decay magnitude by sequence length showing the roughly 10-orders-of-magnitude vanishing effect, plus the computed attention-weight vector for the worked "it" example.

slots.practicalActivity: Implement one full Transformer block in numpy: multi-head scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask, a feed-forward sublayer, residual connections, and layer norm, running it on 5 random "token" embeddings. Prove positional encoding matters by comparing shuffled-input vs. shuffled-output results with and without the sinusoidal positional encoding added, and compute the parameter count for a GPT-2-small-shaped configuration (12 layers, d=768).
slots.deliverable: A script printing the block's output shape, the causal attention-weight matrix for one head, the before/after shuffle-invariance proof, and the computed 124,439,808-parameter total for the GPT-2-small configuration.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's toy bigram "language model" (a V x V logit table trained by gradient descent on 8 invented sentences), track cross-entropy loss and perplexity across training steps, and confirm it converges toward the corpus's own entropy floor. Then run the simulated supervised-fine-tuning step on 4 narrow new sentences and observe both the intended behavior shift and the forgetting effect on the original corpus's loss.
slots.deliverable: A printed loss/perplexity trajectory from the pretraining loop, the next-word probability table after "a" before and after fine-tuning, and a 2-sentence note explaining the forgetting trade-off you observed.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a build_prompt() function that assembles role, task, data, and output-format sections with a few-shot ticket-labeling example, then run the temperature-softmax demo at T=0.2, 1.0, and 2.0 on the same logits to see how randomness changes. Next, build the lesson's bigram hallucination generator from a tiny corpus and flag which generated sentences never appeared in the source text, then evaluate a stand-in classifier on 20 labeled items and compute a 95% Wilson confidence interval around its accuracy.
slots.deliverable: The assembled few-shot prompt string, the 3 temperature-probability distributions, a list of generated sentences marked true/novel, and the computed accuracy point estimate with its Wilson 95% interval.

slots.practicalActivity: Show the one-hot-vector failure (cosine similarity of 0.0 between "car" and "automobile") and then fit TF-IDF + TruncatedSVD (3 components) on the lesson's 15 billing/shipping/login support tickets, confirming that two billing tickets sharing no words rise from a 0.0 TF-IDF cosine to roughly 1.0 in the compressed embedding space.
slots.deliverable: A notebook showing the 0.0 one-hot cosine, the TF-IDF sparse cosine of 0.0 for two paraphrased tickets, and the dense SVD-embedding cosine near 1.0 for the same pair, with a one-sentence explanation of why compression recovered the similarity.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the embed()/compare/rank pipeline on the 15-ticket dataset: fit TF-IDF + SVD once, then embed a brand-new query ("my parcel is late") using only .transform (never refitting), rank all 15 tickets by cosine similarity, and print the top 3. Then normalize the vectors and confirm numerically that cosine, dot product, and squared Euclidean distance all agree on ranking for unit vectors.
slots.deliverable: The top-3 ranked tickets for the new query with their similarity scores, plus the printed equality check (cosine == dot, euclid^2 == 2-2cos) on two normalized ticket vectors.

slots.practicalActivity: Generate 50,000 synthetic 64-dimensional unit vectors in 100 clusters, implement exact brute-force top-10 search as one matrix-vector product, then implement a KMeans-based IVF-style approximate index and sweep nprobe over 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, and 20 clusters. For each setting, measure recall@10 against the exact result and time per query, and decide which nprobe you would ship for a real workload.
slots.deliverable: A table (or chart) of nprobe vs. recall@10 vs. milliseconds-per-query across all 6 settings, plus a one-sentence recommendation of the nprobe value you would choose and why.

slots.practicalActivity: On the same 15-ticket dataset, build both a keyword-search function (TF-IDF cosine) and a semantic-search function (the SVD embedding cosine), write at least 6 of your own test queries with a known correct topic for each, and score both methods with precision@3. Compare the mean precision@3 of keyword vs. semantic search and find at least one query where semantic search wins and one where both fail.
slots.deliverable: A precision@3 score for each method across your test queries, with the specific query where semantic search outperformed keyword search and the specific query where both methods returned nothing useful.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the lesson's 6-chunk policy knowledge base with TF-IDF retrieval and a min_score threshold, write build_prompt() so it returns None when nothing relevant is retrieved, and run it against 3 questions: one that matches a chunk cleanly, one that is a close paraphrase the keyword retriever misses (e.g. "refunded" vs. "Refunds"), and one completely unrelated question that must return None.
slots.deliverable: The 3 assembled (or None) prompts for your test questions, with a one-line note identifying which failure was a lexical-mismatch miss and which was a correct graceful refusal.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the full 5-document retailer-FAQ RAG pipeline from the lesson (index, retrieve with min_score=0.1, assemble a grounded prompt with numbered citations), and run it on all 4 of the lesson's test questions plus 2 of your own. Confirm the retrieval returns the right document for a direct match, returns nothing for an off-topic question, and misses a close paraphrase the way TF-IDF is expected to.
slots.deliverable: Printed retrieval results and assembled prompts for all 6 questions, with a short written note on which question exposed TF-IDF's inability to match paraphrases.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a get_key() helper that reads an API key from an environment variable and raises a clear error if missing, then build the lesson's FakeModel class that fails twice before succeeding, wrap it in a with_retries() exponential-backoff loop, and confirm your call_llm(prompt) function recovers after 2 simulated timeouts. Sketch (do not execute) the matching OpenAI, Anthropic, and Azure OpenAI client call shapes behind the same call_llm interface so a real provider could be swapped in later without touching the rest of your pipeline.
slots.deliverable: A working retry-loop script showing the 2 failed attempts and the successful 3rd call, plus one page of commented, not-executed code showing how each of the 3 providers would plug into the same call_llm(prompt) function.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the validate() function against the category/urgency/order_id schema and run it on the lesson's 5 canned model replies (one clean, one markdown-fenced, one missing a field, one with an invented category, one chatty non-JSON), then wire a retry loop that resubmits the error message until it succeeds or hits max_tries. Separately, build the token-cost estimator across the 3 illustrative pricing tiers and k=2 vs. k=8 retrieved chunks, and write a redact() function that masks an email and a phone number with regex.
slots.deliverable: Pass/fail output for all 5 canned replies plus the retry-success trace, the cost-per-1,000-queries table across tiers and chunk counts, and a tested redact() function with before/after output on a sample sentence.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Build an AI-Powered Data Tool

slots.practicalActivity: Generate the capstone's 300-row synthetic sales table and 7-snippet policy document set from the lesson's seeded functions, write out the 7 test questions (4 data questions, 2 document questions, 1 that must be refused) exactly as the kickoff specifies, and sketch the 4-step architecture (route -> validate -> execute -> answer) with a one-paragraph justification for each of the 4 design decisions: the model never writes code you run, everything the model returns is validated, the tool refuses when unsure, and the LLM is swappable behind one function.
slots.deliverable: The generated sales DataFrame and document list printed to confirm shape, the written list of 7 test questions with their expected routing (data/docs/refuse), and a one-page design-decisions memo.

slots.practicalActivity: Build the full ask() pipeline from the lesson: a fake_llm stub that routes ROUTE:/DATA_ANSWER:/DOCS_ANSWER: prompts, a validate_route() whitelist checker with retry, a run_data() function that only executes model-chosen metric/group_by/filter combinations against real pandas, and the DocSearch TF-IDF retrieval class. Run all 7 kickoff test questions through it, then deliberately break it twice: wrap the stub so its first routing reply is invalid prose (confirm the retry recovers), and make it invent a nonexistent region called "Mars" (confirm validation rejects it safely).
slots.deliverable: Correct answers for all 7 test questions printed from a real run, plus documented output showing the retry-recovery case and the safe-rejection case for the invented region, with one chart of revenue by category generated straight from run_data().

slots.practicalActivity: Write an independent ground-truth check (computed with plain pandas, not your tool's code) for each of the 7 test questions, run them all against your capstone tool, and report a PASS/FAIL count. Then hunt for failures the way the lesson does: find one safe miss (a paraphrase your retrieval cannot match) and one dangerous confident-wrong answer, and write a one-paragraph fix proposal for each. Finish with a README covering problem, architecture, what was real vs. stubbed, results, cost/latency/privacy notes, and next steps.
slots.deliverable: A ground-truth evaluation report (e.g. 7/7 or fewer passed), a documented safe-miss and a documented dangerous-failure case each with a proposed fix, and a complete project README ready to publish to GitHub.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can explain how neural networks, transformers, and LLMs work under the hood, build a working retrieval-augmented-generation pipeline from embeddings through a validated, cost-aware LLM call, and reason honestly about an AI system's limits, cost, latency, and privacy tradeoffs — the modern AI toolkit a data scientist is now expected to bring to any team.
